steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper presenting a new LiDAR point cloud dataset for 3D object detection that covers multiple sensors. Explain the problems with current datasets that motivate it and introduce the dataset and its main properties.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Context: deep learning, autonomous driving, LiDAR, existing 3D datasets
- Problem 1: evaluating across datasets is complex
- Problem 2: sensor diversity is ignored
- Problem 3: domain adaptation mixes scenario and sensor domains
- Our dataset, LiDAR-CS, and its properties

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Context
  - deep learning advanced quickly; supporting hardware improved
  - deep-learning applications more prominent; Autonomous Driving (AD) one of the most noteworthy
  - 3D perception: LiDAR leading choice, reliable range measurement
  - AD 3D perception datasets released: KITTI (cite), nuScene (cite), WOD (cite)

- Cross-dataset evaluation is complex
  - needed to verify generalization; complex, time-consuming
  - (1) different sensors: KITTI Velodyne 64 beams, nuScene 32 beams
  - (2) different labeling rules: KITTI front views only; nuScene, WOD 360° view
  - (3) different categories: KITTI = WOD; nuScene more specific
  - (4) different evaluation metrics -> confusing comparison

- Sensor diversity
  - many LiDAR designs/functions with rapid AD development: Velodyne (cite), Pandora (cite), Livox (cite); many types per manufacturer
  - benchmarks enlarge scenario diversity, ignore sensor diversity; none provide data with different LiDAR sensors
  - Fig. 1: detector performance drops dramatically when train/test sensors differ
  - dataset enlarging sensor diversity helpful

- Domain adaptation
  - crucial challenge in point cloud perception
  - previous work (cite) used multiple datasets
  - ignored: scenario domain and sensor domain both differ across datasets -> two variables, hard to evaluate/analyze approaches
  - easy: various situations with one sensor; hard: identical scenarios with different sensors (background constant, foregrounds changing)

- LiDAR-CS (LiDAR-Cross-Sensors)
  - novel dataset addressing these issues; unique properties vs. existing benchmarks
  - Cross Sensors: 6 types of LiDAR sensors; 6 duplicates per frame, same scenarios and foreground position; only point distribution differs (beam number, field of view, angle resolution, etc.); easy to extend with a new sensor given some real scanned frames
  - Consistent Annotation: same background/foreground for all sensors -> consistent annotations -> same evaluation metric

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Deep learning techniques have advanced quickly in recent years, and the hardware supporting them has improved as well. Because of this, applications related to deep learning have become more prominent, and Autonomous Driving (AD) is one of the most noteworthy of them. For 3D perception tasks, Light Detection and Ranging (LiDAR) sensors have become the leading choice since their range measurement is reliable. To promote the development of the technique, many 3D perception datasets related to AD have been released, such as KITTI, nuScene and WOD.

Even with these notable accomplishments, the community still faces pressing concerns. Evaluating models across different datasets can be complex and needs careful consideration of various factors. This kind of evaluation is usually necessary to verify the generalization ability of a model, but the process is very complex and time-consuming, for several reasons. (1) Different sensors: the LiDAR points are collected with different sensors, e.g., KITTI uses a Velodyne 64 beams LiDAR and nuScene a 32 beams LiDAR. (2) Different labeling rules: the labeling rule is different between datasets, in KITTI only the objects in the front views are annotated while nuScene and WOD are labeled in 360° view. (3) Different categories: KITTI and WOD have the same labeled categories but nuScene defines more specific categories. (4) Different evaluation metrics: also the evaluation metric of each dataset is quite different, and this confuses the comparison over different datasets.

Second, because autonomous driving technology has developed rapidly recently, there are many different LiDAR sensor designs and functions, such as Velodyne, Pandora and Livox, and each manufacturer has lots of LiDAR sensor types. However, the existing LiDAR point cloud benchmarks try to enlarge the scenario diversity and ignore the diversity of sensors. None of them provide more diverse data with different LiDAR sensors. As Fig. 1 shows, the performance of the detectors drops dramatically when training and testing are based on different sensors. So a dataset that enlarges the diversity of sensors would be very helpful for the community.

Third, domain adaptation is a crucial challenge in point cloud perception research. Previous work used multiple datasets to research domain adaptation. But one fact is often ignored, that both the scenario domain and the sensor domain exist across different datasets. Having two variables at the same time makes it difficult to evaluate and analyze different domain adaptation approaches. In most cases it is easy to collect data from various situations with a single sensor. But in real-world applications it becomes challenging to get data with identical scenarios with different sensors, because the background may stay the same while the foregrounds are always changing.

Motivated by these issues, we propose here a novel dataset, LiDAR-CS (LiDAR-Cross-Sensors), which can address them. In general, the LiDAR-CS dataset has the following unique properties compared with existing benchmarks.

Cross Sensors. At the moment LiDAR-CS includes samples from 6 types of LiDAR sensors. For every LiDAR frame we generated 6 duplicates that have the same scenarios and the same foreground position, and the only difference is the point distribution, which comes from inherent attributes of the sensors such as the beam number, field of view, angle resolution, etc. Also, the data can easily be extended with another LiDAR sensor, and only some real scanned frames need to be provided.

Consistent Annotation. Since we generate the data of all the sensors with the same background and foreground, we can keep the annotations consistent for all the sensors. With the same annotation, the evaluation metric can also stay the same for all the data.

steps.name: cited_draft
steps.text:
Deep learning techniques have advanced quickly in recent years, and the hardware supporting them has improved as well. Because of this, applications related to deep learning have become more prominent, and Autonomous Driving (AD) is one of the most noteworthy of them. For 3D perception tasks, Light Detection and Ranging (LiDAR) sensors have become the leading choice since their range measurement is reliable. To promote the development of the technique, many 3D perception datasets related to AD have been released, such as KITTI [1], nuScene [2] and WOD [3].

Even with these notable accomplishments, the community still faces pressing concerns. Evaluating models across different datasets can be complex and needs careful consideration of various factors. This kind of evaluation is usually necessary to verify the generalization ability of a model, but the process is very complex and time-consuming, for several reasons. (1) Different sensors: the LiDAR points are collected with different sensors, e.g., KITTI uses a Velodyne 64 beams LiDAR and nuScene a 32 beams LiDAR. (2) Different labeling rules: the labeling rule is different between datasets, in KITTI only the objects in the front views are annotated while nuScene and WOD are labeled in 360° view. (3) Different categories: KITTI and WOD have the same labeled categories but nuScene defines more specific categories. (4) Different evaluation metrics: also the evaluation metric of each dataset is quite different, and this confuses the comparison over different datasets.

Second, because autonomous driving technology has developed rapidly recently, there are many different LiDAR sensor designs and functions, such as Velodyne [4], Pandora [5] and Livox [6], and each manufacturer has lots of LiDAR sensor types. However, the existing LiDAR point cloud benchmarks try to enlarge the scenario diversity and ignore the diversity of sensors. None of them provide more diverse data with different LiDAR sensors. As Fig. 1 shows, the performance of the detectors drops dramatically when training and testing are based on different sensors. So a dataset that enlarges the diversity of sensors would be very helpful for the community.

Third, domain adaptation is a crucial challenge in point cloud perception research. Previous work [7,8,9] used multiple datasets to research domain adaptation. But one fact is often ignored, that both the scenario domain and the sensor domain exist across different datasets. Having two variables at the same time makes it difficult to evaluate and analyze different domain adaptation approaches. In most cases it is easy to collect data from various situations with a single sensor. But in real-world applications it becomes challenging to get data with identical scenarios with different sensors, because the background may stay the same while the foregrounds are always changing.

Motivated by these issues, we propose here a novel dataset, LiDAR-CS (LiDAR-Cross-Sensors), which can address them. In general, the LiDAR-CS dataset has the following unique properties compared with existing benchmarks.

Consistent Annotation. Since we generate the data of all the sensors with the same background and foreground, we can keep the annotations consistent for all the sensors. With the same annotation, the evaluation metric can also stay the same for all the data.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
In recent years, deep learning techniques have advanced quickly, and the hardware that supports them has also improved. As a result, deep-learning-related applications have become more prominent, and one of the most noteworthy is Autonomous Driving (AD). For 3D perception tasks, Light Detection and Ranging (LiDAR) sensors have become the leading choice due to their reliable range measurement. To promote the development of the technique, many AD-related 3D perception datasets have been released, such as KITTI [1], nuScene [2] and WOD [3].

Despite these notable accomplishments, pressing concerns still confront the community. Evaluating models across different datasets can be a complex task that requires careful consideration of various factors. This kind of evaluation is usually necessary to verify a model's generalization ability; however, the process is very complex and time-consuming for several reasons: (1) different sensors. The LiDAR points are collected from different sensors, e.g., KITTI (Velodyne 64 beams LiDAR), nuScene (32 beams LiDAR); (2) different labeling rules. In the KITTI dataset only the objects in the front views have been annotated, while nuScene and WOD are labeled in 360° view; (3) different categories. KITTI and WOD share the same labeled categories while nuScene defines more specific categories; (4) different evaluation metrics. Last but not least, the evaluation metric for each dataset is also quite different, which confuses the comparison over different datasets.

Secondly, due to the rapid recent development of autonomous driving technology, there are many different LiDAR sensor designs and functions, such as Velodyne [4], Pandora [5] and Livox [6], and each manufacturer has lots of LiDAR sensor types. However, the existing LiDAR point cloud benchmarks try to enlarge the scenario diversity while the diversity of sensors has been ignored; none of them provide more diverse data with different LiDAR sensors. As shown in Fig. 1, the detectors' performances drop dramatically when the training and the testing are based on different sensors. Therefore, a dataset that can enlarge the sensor diversity will be very helpful for the community.

Thirdly, domain adaptation is a crucial challenge in point cloud perception research. Previous work [7,8,9] employed multiple datasets for domain adaptation research. However, one fact is often ignored: both the scenario domain and the sensor domain exist across different datasets. The existence of two variables at the same time makes it difficult to evaluate and analyze different domain adaptation approaches. In most cases, it is easy to collect data from various situations using a single sensor, but it becomes challenging to obtain data with identical scenarios using different sensors in real-world applications, because the background may stay constant while the foregrounds are constantly changing.

Motivated by the issues mentioned above, a novel LiDAR-CS (LiDAR-Cross-Sensors) dataset is proposed here which can address these issues. In general, compared with existing benchmarks, the LiDAR-CS dataset has the following unique properties.

Cross Sensors. Currently, LiDAR-CS includes samples from 6 types of LiDAR sensors. For each LiDAR frame, we have generated 6 duplicates with the same scenarios and the same foreground position; the only difference is the point distribution, which comes from the inherent attributes of the sensors, such as the beam number, field of view, angle resolution, etc. In addition, the data can easily be extended by adding another LiDAR sensor, needing only some real scanned frames.

Consistent Annotation. We generate all the sensors' data with the same background and foreground, so we can keep consistent annotations for all the sensors. With the same annotation, the evaluation metric can remain the same for all the data.

References:
[1] A. Geiger, P. Lenz, and R. Urtasun, “Are we ready for autonomous driving? the kitti vision benchmark suite,” in CVPR , 2012, pp. 3354–3361.
[2] H. Caesar, V. Bankiti, A. H. Lang, S. Vora, V. E. Liong, Q. Xu, A. Krishnan, Y. Pan, G. Baldan, and O. Beijbom, “nuscenes: A multimodal dataset for autonomous driving,” in CVPR , 2020, pp. 11 621–11 631.
[3] P. Sun, H. Kretzschmar, X. Dotiwalla, A. Chouard, V. Patnaik, P. Tsui, J. Guo, Y. Zhou, Y. Chai, B. Caine, et al. , “Scalability in perception for autonomous driving: Waymo open dataset,” in CVPR , 2020, pp. 2446–2454.
[4] “Velodyne lidar,” https://velodynelidar.com/ .
[5] “Hesai tech,” https://www.hesaitech.com/en/ .
[6] “Livox tech,” https://www.livoxtech.com/ .
[7] Y. Wang, X. Chen, Y. You, L. E. Li, B. Hariharan, M. Campbell, K. Q. Weinberger, and W.-L. Chao, “Train in germany, test in the usa: Making 3d object detectors generalize,” in CVPR , 2020, pp. 11 713–11 723.
[8] J. Yang, S. Shi, Z. Wang, H. Li, and X. Qi, “St3d: Self-training for unsupervised domain adaptation on 3d object detection,” in CVPR , 2021, pp. 10 368–10 378.
[9] B. Zhang, J. Yuan, B. Shi, T. Chen, Y. Li, and Y. Qiao, “Uni3d: A unified baseline for multi-dataset 3d object detection,” in Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition , 2023, pp. 9253–9262.
